title: How LARP Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss LARP (live action role playing), drawing on a How Stuff Works article by Tracy Wilson and an interview with game designer Laurie Zolkowski, creator of the larp King's Gate. They cover how larps are designed (rules, universes, combat via foam-and-PVC "boffers," spells, hit points, resurrection), the roles of player characters versus non-player characters and game staff, the three game types (battle, theatrical, role playing), the three player mindsets (dramatists, gamists, immersionists) from Peter Brockman's essay, the community and social aspects, and the logistics of running games. The episode also includes a listener mail segment about cap gras syndrome (Capgras delusion) and a murder case in a house a listener's family moved into.
topics: magic and spell rules in larp

segments.title: Opening banter and D&D follow-up
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, framing LARP as a further step from Dungeons and Dragons table play, and introduce the source article by Tracy Wilson and her interview with Laurie Zolkowski.

segments.title: What LARP is and King's Gate
segments.summary: LARP stands for live action role playing, usually fantasy-based, with players in costume acting out role playing games physically. Laurie Zolkowski's game King's Gate was sold to Red Button Productions, and she spent a year or more creating it.

segments.title: Designing a larp universe and rules
segments.summary: Designing a larp means creating a whole fictional universe with races, classes, magic, and weapons, plus rules for combat, armor class, hit points, and simulated death. Designers can adapt existing rule systems.

segments.title: Player characters, NPCs, and game staff
segments.summary: Non-player characters such as innkeepers or bandits advance the story, while player characters pursue goals and develop skills. Game staff include a game master, plot committee, and administrators. Campaigns span multiple weekend games that change the world.

segments.title: Three types of larp games
segments.summary: The hosts describe battle games with boffer weapons, theatrical games such as Fiasco and Vampire the Masquerade where conflicts are resolved by rock-paper-scissors, and role playing games that combine battle and story. Darkon is cited as a popular battle larp and documentary.

segments.title: Combat, magic, death and resurrection rules
segments.summary: Players call out damage they inflict, magic requires an incantation and a physical hit with a bean bag or bird seed pouch, and characters can die and be resurrected within limits. Life ring tags and non-participation areas help track status.

segments.title: Larp community, mindsets, and logistics
segments.summary: Larpers are described as imaginative and sometimes socially different, and the larp appeals to people seeking confidence. Peter Brockman's three-way model defines dramatists, gamists, and immersionists, with administrators also noted. Logistics such as permits and insurance are discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail: cap gras syndrome murder house
segments.summary: A listener describes moving into a Michigan house where a son had murdered his parents, and says the son claimed his parents were impostors due to Capgras syndrome. The hosts also discuss a New Jersey parricide case and invite listener feedback.
